stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about unattributed evidence. untraceable claims should be traced or marked unverified. A marginal reminder adds: trace or mark unverified. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The passage above presents a case and the terms needed to judge it. Based only on what the passage establishes about unattributed evidence, which choice holds up?

options.text: Trace or mark it unverified
Keep repeating it as fact
Add a plausible source name
Ask patients to verify it

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: untraceable claims should be traced or marked unverified. On that basis "Trace or mark it unverified" is the supported choice. Option B ("Keep repeating it as fact") fails because it propagates an untraceable claim; Option C ("Add a plausible source name") fails because it fabricates a citation; Option D ("Ask patients to verify it") fails because it shifts verification to patients.
questions.hint: Trace or mark unverified.

stimulus.body: A handover says everyone agrees the new alarm is too sensitive. No names or roles are given, and the alarm's false-alarm rate is not recorded. The team must respond. vague consensus needs specifics and data. A marginal reminder adds: get specifics and a rate. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: The question turns on what the note above shows about vague attribution. Given the proposal "Remove the alarm because everyone agrees", which choice is consistent with the evidence in the passage?

options.text: Ignore the complaint entirely
Remove the alarm because everyone agrees
Ask who specifically and record the false-alarm rate
Tell everyone they are wrong

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: the passage gives the controlling distinction: vague consensus needs specifics and data. On that basis "Ask who specifically and record the false-alarm rate" is the supported choice. Option A ("Ignore the complaint entirely") fails because it dismisses a possibly valid concern; Option B ("Remove the alarm because everyone agrees") fails because it acts on vague consensus; Option D ("Tell everyone they are wrong") fails because it responds with assertion not inquiry.
questions.hint: Get specifics and a rate.

questions.learningObjective: Ask for the definition behind a rate

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: Rates need a clear definition. A marginal reminder adds: define what counts as a fall. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The note above supplies the evidence for a judgment about bare statistics. One proposed reading is "Assume all falls are counted". Which of the four options is actually supported by the passage?

options.text: Accept 5 percent as comparable
options.misconception: treats "Accept 5 percent as comparable" as if it followed from the evidence

options.text: Round 5 percent to 10 percent
Assume all falls are counted
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reasoning the passage sets out

options.text: Ask how a fall is defined and counted

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: close reading of the note yields this rule: rates need a clear definition. On that basis "Ask how a fall is defined and counted" is the supported choice. Option A ("Accept 5 percent as comparable") fails because it treats "Accept 5 percent as comparable" as if it followed from the evidence; Option B ("Round 5 percent to 10 percent") fails because it distorts the figure arbitrarily; Option C ("Assume all falls are counted") fails because it reverses the direction of the reasoning that settles bare statistics.
questions.hint: Define what counts as a fall.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid absolute claims from limited data

stimulus.body: A short reference note on hedging and assertion is set for a close-reading task. It states: Two weeks cannot support eliminates all. A marginal reminder adds: soften absolutes from short data. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The passage above presents a case and the terms needed to judge it. Based only on what the passage establishes about hedging and assertion, which choice holds up?

options.text: Keep eliminates because two weeks passed
options.misconception: lets a short window justify absolutism

options.text: Remove the rota entirely
Soften to reduced overtime in two weeks
Add always to strengthen the claim

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: two weeks cannot support eliminates all. On that basis "Soften to reduced overtime in two weeks" is the supported choice. Option A ("Keep eliminates because two weeks passed") fails because it lets a short window justify absolutism; Option B ("Remove the rota entirely") fails because it overreacts to limited data; Option D ("Add always to strengthen the claim") fails because it strengthens wording without basis.
questions.hint: Soften absolutes from short data.
